entries.title: Trump bars CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump has accused CNN, MS NOW and Politico of spreading fake news.
entries.content:
Politics

United States of America

Trump bars CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House

September 18, 2026

US President Donald Trump has accused CNN, MS NOW and Politico of spreading fake news.

Advertisement

US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is banning major US media outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House.

In a post on Truth Social, he accused them of spreading fake news. He also indicated that other media outlets may also be ejected from the White House.

More to follow...

entries.title: Iran's 'new Hezbollah:' How powerful are the Houthis now?
entries.summary: After Houthi victories in Yemen, the group's importance in the US-Iran war has grown. Previously Lebanon's Hezbollah was considered most significant in Iran's "axis of resistance." Now the Houthis are rising to the top.
entries.content:
Yemen

Iran's 'new Hezbollah:' How powerful are the Houthis now?

September 18, 2026

After Houthi victories in Yemen, the group's importance in the US-Iran war has grown. Previously Lebanon's Hezbollah was considered most significant in Iran's "axis of resistance." Now the Houthis are rising to the top.

After recent events in Yemen, a small crowd marched down an Iraqi street holding signs that were almost identical to those seen not too long ago further south.

The signs said, "death to America" and insulted Saudi Arabia and Israel, with slogans very similar to those used by the Houthi rebel group in Yemen. The men in the Iraqi video are members of one of Iraq's Shiite Muslim paramilitary groups.

Both the Iraqi paramilitaries and the Houthi group in Yemen are part of what is known as the "axis of resistance" in the Middle East, groups supported by Iran that often act at Iran's behest. Other members are Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza.

After the US and Israel began attacking Iran in late February 2026, "axis of resistance" members responded by targeting sites associated with the US or Israel. But up until recently, the Houthi group had remained more or less on the sidelines.

However their latest military campaign, which has seen Houthi fighters take further control of the Yemeni coast and several islands in the Red Sea, "sets up conditions to establish… an axis of resistance-controlled body of water as part of [an] effort to assert control over regional oil exports," US-based research organization the Institute for the Study of War explained last week.

Iran and the US are already fighting for control over the Strait of Hormuz, another important waterway for oil exports and trade.

In Iran, hardline regime-supporting newspapers published laudatory articles about the Houthis' territorial gains.

The gains "greatly increased the weight of Sanaa [the Yemeni capital, under Houthi control] as a branch of resistance in the ongoing regional war," one of Iran's most conservative newspapers, Kayhan, wrote.

Supporters of the Iranian government have been holding nightly gatherings in major cities across the country since the US-Iran war began and this week, at the 200th such event, crowds chanted "you are my soul, O Yemen!"

The 'new Hezbollah?'

This was the kind of praise previously lavished on another "axis of resistance" group, Hezbollah. But Hezbollah's armed faction, degraded by recent Israeli attacks and the loss of their base in Syria, looks less intimidating these days.

And the Houthis now appear to be doing things that Hezbollah couldn't — for example, bringing down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet this week using a missile the group said it modified itself. Hezbollah has managed to shoot down large Israeli drones and has targeted fighter jets but never hit any.

Could the Houthis be taking Hezbollah's place as the potentially most important and possibly even more dangerous force in the "axis of resistance?"

The Houthis haven't had to fight Israel — they are too far away geographically.

"But I think they [the Houthis] have become more valuable than Hezbollah could ever be," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow focused on Yemen at UK think tank Chatham House. "Of course, Hezbollah had decades of experience and was the one who built the Houthis' capacity over years. But the Houthis have now exceeded them."

The Houthis are "increasingly performing a similar strategic function for Iran [as Hezbollah] and in some respects a more useful one," confirms Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King's College London.

"Hezbollah gave Tehran deterrence against Israel from Lebanon. The Houthis give Iran leverage over Saudi Arabia, Israel and global shipping," he told DW. "So I think their strategic importance to Tehran has risen sharply as Hezbollah has come under much greater pressure."

Al-Muslimi notes that Houthi leaders, including current chief Abdul Malik al-Houthi, were devoted fans of Hezbollah leader Nassan Hasrallah, killed by Israel in 2024 and seen as a hero because of his organization's part in forcing Israel to withdraw from Lebanon in 2000.

"You can see how he even tries to imitate Nasrallah in his speeches," al-Muslimi, who co-founded the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, told DW. "And now Abdul Malik al-Houthi has more leverage than Nasrallah ever had."

Nasrallah was once seen as "the fixer" for the "axis of resistance," he notes, a leader who acted as a conduit between the different factions, giving orders to Iran-supported fighters in Lebanon, Yemen and Syria.

Al-Houthi is likely moving into that role now, al-Muslimi believes, pointing to the fact that one recent attack on Saudi pipelines actually came from Iraqi axis members.

Iranian proxy or ally?

Unlike with Hezbollah though, there's still disagreement over exactly how much control Iran has over them.

A review of press by the Iraq-based outlet Amwaj showed that while Iranian media celebrated Houthi gains as a victory for Iran's "axis of resistance," Houthi-run channels were more focused on their own fight against Saudi Arabia, which has set up a blockade on Houthi-controlled territories.

Krieg believes the biggest difference between the Houthis and Hezbollah is autonomy.

"The Houthis… have their own leadership, ideology, domestic constituency and territorial project," he pointed out. "Tehran can enable them, arm them and benefit from their actions, but it cannot necessarily switch them on and off at will."

Other observers note that in the past, the Houthis moved ahead with certain military plans despite objections from Iran. Tehran has also denied having anything to do with this latest campaign.

But al-Muslimi isn't so sure. He says that over the past two years, the Houthis have come a lot closer to Iran. There are regular reports of Iran sending sophisticated weaponry to the Houthis. In July, sources inside Iran told Reuters news agency that Iranian leadership had discussed with the Houthis having them close off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

"Even as Houthi leaders frame their actions in local terms, their alignment with Tehran appears to have tightened," Allison Minor, previously the US deputy special envoy for Yemen, said in Foreign Affairs magazine last week.

Can the Houthis be beaten?

The one thing everyone does agree on is that the Houthis will be hard to rein in. Past military campaigns by Saudi Arabia, the US and other countries have failed. Sanctions and economic pressure tend not to impact either because the Houthis don't operate within the international financial system.

The Houthis take a "zero sum approach," al-Muslimi explains. They collect taxes but don't pay salaries or provide public services; everything goes towards fighting. The group's founding father argued that contemporary Muslim societies were too "soft," and that poverty and hardship are a divine test.

That's very different from Hezbollah: The Lebanese group also has a political branch at home, and offers social welfare services. It must also carefully balance relationships with other demographic groups in Lebanon.

The Houthis have none of those restraints.

"They don't care if the Israelis bomb the airport or the US bombs a hospital," al-Muslimi says. "It actually serves them very well because their ideology is all about martyrdom and sacrifice."

Which, he suggests, makes them potentially more dangerous than Hezbollah, especially for Yemeni civilians.

"They are a major international threat," he agrees, "but they're the biggest threat ever to the idea of a republic and citizenship in Yemen's history."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Ryanair boss apologizes for calling other airlines 'rapists'
entries.summary: The airline CEO had used the term to describe other airlines with high fares. His comments were criticized by officials both in Ireland and the UK.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

The airline CEO had used the term to describe other airlines with high fares. His comments were criticized by officials both in Ireland and the UK.

Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary "sincerely and unreservedly" apologized on Friday for recent remarks in which he described other airlines as "rapists" because of their high fares.

O'Leary said 'careless' remarks caused 'considerable upset and offense'

"I have come to realize, however, that the word I used too carelessly has caused considerable upset and offense to a wide number of people, especially victims and survivors," O'Leary said in a video posted online.

It's a U-turn from earlier, when O'Leary refused to apologize for the comments. Dublin Rape Crisis Centre chief executive Rachel Morrogh said O'Leary trivialized rape with the remarks.

"Since I certainly did not trivialize the heinous crime of rape, I will certainly not be issuing any apology," O'Leary said last week.

O'Leary had originally made the remarks to journalists at Ryanair's company headquarters in Ireland.

"You might find some people will choose not to fly with Ryanair — but you know they'll be overrun with the people abandoning Aer Lingus, Lufthansa, BA, and others desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with high-fare rapists around Europe," O'Leary said.  

O'Leary's remarks met with backlash in Ireland, UK

O'Leary is one of Ireland's richest and most prominent businesspeople. His "rapist" remarks were met with criticism from leaders both in Ireland and the UK.  

Ireland's Taoiseach Michael Martin said he was "disappointed" by O'Leary's comments and added the Ryanair chief "should just stand back and reflect and listen to the voice of women" regarding the issue.

Martin told RTE Radio One that rape is "an awful, awful violation of a person, which leaves a terrible trauma." However, the Irish leader of the centrist to center-right Fianna Fail party did not call on O'Leary to explicitly apologize.

Ireland's deputy prime minister, or Tanaiste, Simon Harris said O'Leary's comments were an "inappropriate use of language." However, Harris of the center-right Fine Gael party also did not explicitly call on O'Leary to apologize.

Laura Harmon, a senator belonging to Ireland's center-left opposition Labour Party, said O'Leary must apologize for the comments. "The casual use of the word 'rapist' to describe prices of his competitors is deeply shocking and could be traumatizing for any survivor of sexual abuse," Harmon said.

The UK's Transport Minister Heidi Alexander of the British Labour Party, in comments to LBC radio, said "Mr. O'Leary is often quick to share his considered thoughts with me and with the wider world." 

"I would say that women who have been raped and who have been subjected to such appalling violence, I'm not sure they're going to be rushing to book tickets with him, let's be honest," Alexander said.

O'Leary had earlier made controversial remarks regarding obese and Muslim passengers. He had also floated a fee for using a toilet mid-flight and expressed climate denial. 

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Strait of Hormuz attacks spill oil into Persian Gulf
entries.summary: As war disrupts one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, satellite images reveal that oil is spreading toward protected coral reefs and mangrove forests.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

As war disrupts one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, satellite images reveal that oil is spreading toward protected coral reefs and mangrove forests.

A dark, muddied patch of blue, incongruent with the rest of the ocean; a winding thread of silvery white; a reflective metallic sheen — these are some of the telltale signs on a satellite image that oil may be leaking into the water.

Experts have identified these and many other visual signaturesin the Strait of Hormuz, leading them to conclude that there's an environmental crisis playing out amid the US-Iran war, as tankers are struck by missiles, set on fire or sunk.

One recent example: In June, a Russian tanker carrying about 800,000 barrels of oil stranded off the coast of Oman, causing a major spill.

Earlier in the war, there were as many as 85 large oil-laden tankers stuck in the Strait — that number has since dropped to 13, according to Greenpeace. Each stranded tanker, plus every other vessel trying to move through the waterway, poses a distinct risk for attack and thus a spill. Since the start of the war, the environmental organization has used satellite imagery to track more than 100 spills.

There are likely several other spills that we don't know of, amid widespread GPS spoofing in the region that causes ships to broadcast false positions. Greenpeace released a report this week calling the situation an "ecological catastrophe" and pinpointing a number of oil slicks that are extending into protected and fragile ecosystems. 

"People should be concerned," Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief, told DW. The war has taken "a very, very heavy toll on the environment," she said, with the damage now reaching new scales.

Where is the oil spreading?

Greenpeace identified five major oil slicks earlier this week with a total visible area of 240 square kilometers (about 90 square miles) in the Strait of Hormuz. That's about four times the size of Manhattan.

These patches of oil floating on the ocean's surface are getting smaller — now about 80 square kilometers — according to more up-to-date satellite images, as weather conditions have likely made the slicks disperse. But that does not mean the ecological impact is any less severe, Noelle said. "Oil can also sink into the sediment and impact the ecosystems for years and years."

What's concerning is where the slicks were identified. One was found near Musandam National Park, a protected area in Oman that's home to coral reefs, sea life and important breeding grounds for sea birds. Another is close to Iran's Minab River Delta and its protected mudflats and mangrove forests. This kind of damage can take decades for ecosystems to recover from.

Tracking an unclear picture

It's hard to say exactly how far the oil has reached and how severe the damage is.

"What we have put out is the conservative estimate," Noelle said. "It might be worse. It's definitely not better."

Greenpeace and other environmental organizations are relying on satellite images provided by the Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites. They're part of the European Union's Earth observation program and are publicly available.

There are also private satellite providers such as Planet Labs that tend to have higher-resolution images. But they've limited access to satellite imagery during the war to prevent their data from being used for military targeting. And there are limits to on-the-ground reports too. 

"We don't have a lot of information coming from the country itself, both in Iran as well as the Gulf states," Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher who uses open-source methods at the Dutch peace organization Pax, told DW. "There is quite restrictive policies of people posting imagery from what's happening on the shore."

The toll on wildlife and people

Oil pooling into the Gulf poses a number of threats — both to biodiversity and to humans.

Oil can be deadly for seabirds. It coats their feathers, reducing their natural waterproofing and buoyancy, making it harder to stay afloat, fly, and hunt for food. Even small amounts of oil can damage eggs too, causing them not to hatch or to be born with deformities.

Mangrove habitats, which provide safe harbor for coastal species, are also hit hard.

"Mangroves have aerial roots, and the oil is covering these roots like a film and actually hindering the mangroves in exchanging gases," Noelle said. "They're kind of suffocated by the oil. Most of the time, it leads to the trees dying."

The risks extend to people, as well. Coastal communities rely on fish that die off after being exposed to oil. And oil spills contaminate water used for Gulf states' drinking supply. Desalination — or converting seawater into drinkable water — is where 90% of drinking water in Kuwait comes from, along with about 86% in Oman and 70% in Saudi Arabia.

Cleanup is no easy fix.

"It's unlikely that it will be addressed quickly, because of the war," Zwijnenburg said. "War in general makes it very difficult to respond fast to these kind of emergencies. There are a range of limitations because of the military movement, because of mines — so it's very difficult to get vessels and cleanup operations to start."

Environmental groups have pointed to the war in Iran — and the rising scale of oil spills it has caused — as further evidence that the world needs to move away from its dependence on fossil fuels.

"The most sustainable long-term damage prevention for things like that would be to reduce and ultimately end our dependency on oil and gas," Noelle said. "Because, as long as our energy systems and transport routes are centered around fossil fuels, there will be a continued environmental risk." 

Edited by: Sarah Steffen

entries.title: Ebola: DR Congo outbreak not slowing, MSF warns
entries.summary: Doctors Without Borders has warned against premature optimism amid the DRC's largest-ever Ebola outbreak. "The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving," an MSF official said, entering new and more underprepared regions.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

Doctors Without Borders has warned against premature optimism amid the DRC's largest-ever Ebola outbreak. "The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving," an MSF official said, entering new and more underprepared regions.

Medical charity Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on Friday that "the race to contain the Ebola disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is far from over." 

MSF issued the comments after DRC's government and the World Health Organization (WHO) had both spoken of signs of slowing transmission in some places earlier this week, prompting some relatively upbeat headlines and coverage.

The outbreak, which was first declared in mid-May but likely started spreading several months earlier, is the largest in DRC's national history and the fastest-spreading on record anywhere. 

What did MSF say about the outbreak and its spread?

MSF — which has around 1,700 staff in the DRC, most of them Congolese — warned that while the observed spread was slowing in the initial epicenter of Ituri province, the number of new cases being recorded had not fallen on a national level.

"Assuming the outbreak is under control because some Ebola treatment centers are admitting fewer patients would be a mistake," MSF's emergency coordinator in DRC Anthony Kergosien said.

"The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving: South Ubangi has become the seventh affected province, while North Kivu now accounts for nearly half of all newly confirmed cases, with test positivity rising sharply in recent days," Kergosien said.

He added that undetected chains of transmission had already taken hold in the worst-hit areas, and said "the spread of the outbreak into new areas with even weaker preparedness and response capacities poses a serious risk."

Which factors helped DRC's worst Ebola outbreak spread so fast?

The deadly virus has killed more than 3,500 people from more than 7,200 confirmed cases since the outbreak was declared in May, according to WHO figures.

Based on the recorded data, the quality of which is gradually improving with the passage of time, the 2026 outbreak is the fastest-spreading in history.

It's also the largest in the DRC's history, second in overall size only to the West African outbreak of 2013-2016. The West African outbreak needed around two and a half years to reach a caseload of more than 28,000, not four months to pass 7,000.

Many of the cases have been concentrated in hard-to-reach areas in DRC's north and east long plagued by instability, poor health infrastructure and a series of armed groups.

Medical staff strikes have also contributed to problems fighting the spread, as have dearly-held funeral and burial traditions that pose the risk of post-mortem transmission as people bid their loved ones farewell.

The outbreak also involves a rare Ebolavirus strain, Bundibugyo, meaning that existing treatments and vaccines — several of which are prohibitively expensive by the standards of the region anyway — were untested and of uncertain value against it.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Airport malaria in Germany remains infrequent
entries.summary: An outbreak of malaria at Frankfurt Airport this summer has raised alarm. Experts believe parasites probably arrived in a passenger's luggage. But with the onset of fall, the risks of contracting the disease are low.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

An outbreak of malaria at Frankfurt Airport this summer has raised alarm. Experts believe parasites probably arrived in a passenger's luggage. But with the onset of fall, the risks of contracting the disease are low.

Eight people are known to have contracted malaria in the vicinity of Frankfurt Airport in central Germany since July; three of them have died. Those affected are mostly employees of the airport operator Fraport.

The Frankfurt Public Health Department believes the outbreak is due to "airport malaria," which occurs when a female Anopheles mosquito carrying the malaria parasite travels by aircraft to a country where the disease is not common from one where it is, bites a person and infects their red blood cells. 

"We are dealing with a very rare occurrence, not a new frequent disease in Germany," said Achim Hörauf, the director of the Institute for Medical Microbiology, Immunology and Parasitology at Bonn's University Hospital (UKB), in a press release.

Airport malaria is very infrequent

The last documented case of airport malaria in Germany before the current ones was in 2023, according to the Epidemiologisches Bulletin of the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an online journal that regularly provides information on infectious diseases and public health.

Normally, those with the disease in Germany were infected elsewhere and brought it back during a long-haul trip.

But a mosquito can make its way to Germany as a "stowaway" if it was trapped in a suitcase or in clothing. Hörauf said that under certain circumstances, it might be able to survive in warmer areas of an airport.

Frankfurt cases are of dangerous malaria tropica

According to a UKB press release, the cases in Frankfurt involve malaria tropica, which is considered to be the most dangerous and potentially life-threatening form of malaria.

To contract the disease, a person needs to be bitten by a female anopheles mosquito infected with the Plasmodium falciparum parasite. This pathogen passes to the human and then attacks the red blood vessels.

"Simply put, it can lead to many small blockages in the blood vessels," explained Hörauf. "Depending on which organ is affected, various serious complications can arise."

Fluid can accumulate in the lungs, or neurological damage can result if the blood vessels of the brain are affected. Acute kidney failure is also possible. About 20% of those affected die if the disease is left untreated.

"If a diagnosis is made in time, there can be targeted treatment," Hörauf said. "If the disease is overlooked, however, it can very quickly take a severe turn."

At first, symptoms are not specific, resembling those of the flu: sudden high fever, chills, headaches and muscle pain. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are also possible.

Frankfurt authorities tell public to seek advice in case of symptoms

The Frankfurt Public Health Department has advised anybody who lives or works near Frankfurt Airport to seek medical attention immediately if they experience any such symptoms.

Rapid diagnostic tests can provide evidence of malaria in human blood and then a blood test can help to confirm this. The RKI says treatment should take place at a hospital, which has expertise in tropical medicine.

As summer comes to an end and temperatures cool in Germany, particularly at night, the conditions are becoming less favorable for mosquitoes and malaria parasites.

However, experts warn that there could still be other cases of malaria in Germany despite the cooler weather. Plasmodium falciparum has an incubation period of seven to 15 days, so more than two weeks can pass between a mosquito transmitting malaria to somebody by biting them and the onset of symptoms. According to Hörauf, the biggest challenge is to ensure that people think malaria could be a possibility even if they have not traveled abroad.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Fact Check: False video alleges Berlin votes destroyed
entries.summary: A video claiming to show AfD postal ballots being destroyed has gone viral ahead of Berlin's September 20 election. DW Fact Check examines the footage, the accounts sharing it and how widely it is really being viewed.
entries.content:
Germany

Fact Check: False video alleges Berlin votes destroyed

September 18, 2026

A video claiming to show AfD postal ballots being destroyed has gone viral ahead of Berlin's September 20 election. DW Fact Check examines the footage, the accounts sharing it and how widely it is really being viewed.

Berliners will vote in state and district elections on September 20. In the days leading up to the vote, a video circulated on social media that allegedly shows a man opening postal voting envelopes and destroying ballots cast for the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD).

DW Fact check reviewed more than a dozen posts sharing the footage. The posts use similar captions, presenting the video as evidence of election fraud in Germany. Several have amassed hundreds of thousands of views on X.

How widely has the video spread? And is its reach driven by genuine public interest? Or is something else boosting its visibility? DW Fact check investigated the video and the accounts sharing it.

Claim: A video shows a man destroying AfD ballots in Berlin with a carpet knife.

One post sharing the footage claims:

"A video circulating in Berlin shows a man opening mail-in voting envelopes and destroying ballots marked for the AfD, while ballots for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU are left intact. The footage appeared days after the AfD's landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Berlin holds its state election on September 20."

The post had received about 327,000 views when DW Fact Check reviewed it on September 18.

DW Fact check: False

At first glance, the ballot paper appears authentic. Its names and layout match those of the official ballot paper for the Spandau 2 constituency in western Berlin, which is publicly available online. However, there are several inconsistencies in the documents shown in the video.

Berlin's state returning officer, Stephan Bröchler, told DW that the documents shown in the video are not authentic election papers from Berlin.

Bröchler said the envelopes shown in the video did not match the official ones used for this election. Bröchler also noted that the way the envelopes are sealed appears suspicious.

According to official guidelines issued by Berlin's election authorities, postal voters receive a voting package containing a "Wahlschein," or a voter declaration that needs to be signed, plus two envelopes and the ballot papers for the elections. For the September 20 vote, Berliners receive two ballot papers: a grey-and-blue ballot for the election to the city-state House of Representatives and an orange ballot for their District Assembly. 

In the video, however, the documents do not correspond to the official postal voting package. The person in the video opens a red envelope and removes a white envelope. The signed voter declaration is missing. Without it, a mail-in ballot would be invalid.

The person then takes out only the grey-and-blue ballot paper for the Berlin House of Representatives from the white envelope.

Although voters may choose to vote in only one of the two elections, it would be unusual for three envelopes in succession to contain only one ballot paper. However, the footage does not clearly show whether the second envelope is really empty.

Another detail raises doubts about the video's authenticity: In the background, large grey bins allegedly containing postal ballots are marked with a version of Berlin's coat of arms featuring the Berlin bear.

Bröchler said such features were not used by Berlin's election authorities.

"Marking the ballot boxes with a Berlin bear is also unknown and uncommon here," he said.

Bröchler's conclusion is clear: "It can be ruled out that any actual Berlin election documents are involved. The video is clearly intended to discredit postal voting."

Has the video really gone viral?

One of the accounts that shared the video has previously come under scrutiny. An investigation by the Lithuania-based research organization Debunk linked the account to the so-called "Sprinter" network, a group of X accounts. The researchers identified what they described as signs of coordinated and inauthentic activity, including unusually high posting volumes, frequent account renaming and evidence of purchased followers. Debunk said the network was used to amplify pro-Kremlin narratives.

DW Fact check reviewed more than 15 other posts sharing the footage, many of them using nearly identical captions. Together, the posts had accumulated more than 3.2 million views by the time DW Fact check examined them.

The accounts sharing the video also showed several suspicious characteristics. Almost all of the 15 accounts examined exhibited at least one sign of potentially inauthentic behavior, including rapid follower growth, frequent username changes or limited evidence of normal user engagement.

One account, which presented itself as an independent media company based in West Asia, had more than 43,000 followers despite having been created only in April 2026. During that period, the account changed its username nine times.

On their own, these characteristics do not prove that the accounts are coordinated or that the video's engagement was entirely artificially generated. They do, however, show that the video's apparent reach should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of widespread, organic discussion on X.

A pattern seen before

The video resembles other false election-related claims that have circulated about Germany in recent months.

Ahead of the September 6 election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, DW Fact check examined a video that similarly purported to show AfD postal ballots being destroyed. The claim was false. 

Among other inconsistencies, all three crossed-out ballots shown in the footage carried the same name on the signed voter declaration. The envelopes had already been opened, and the ballots lacked a hole punch required for use with voting templates designed for blind and visually impaired voters.

DW Fact check has also investigated and debunked numerous other false claims targeting Germany's postal voting system.

Julia Smirnova, who investigates influence operations as a researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), told DW that these similarities, together with the way the new video is being disseminated, indicate that it is "highly likely" to be part of the Storm-1516 influence operation.

German security authorities and researchers have attributed Storm-1516 to Russia. 

The operation has previously used fabricated videos, forged documents and purported eyewitness accounts to spread false narratives about elections and other political issues.

In February 2025, Germany's Interior Ministry said it had indications that two fake videos alleging manipulation of AfD ballots were connected to the Storm 1516 campaign, citing similarities in their content and distribution.

Edited by: Thomas Sparrow

entries.title: Zelenskyy holds inaugural 'Carpathian Eight' regional summit
entries.summary: Zelenskyy said the summit was a "significant beginning" of a movement to strengthen ties with its neighboring countries.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Zelenskyy holds inaugural 'Carpathian Eight' regional summit

September 18, 2026

Zelenskyy said the summit was a "significant beginning" of a movement to strengthen ties with its neighboring countries.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday welcomed the leaders and representatives of Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary to work on deepening cooperation. The European Union was also involved in the talks.

The summit took place in the western Ukrainian ski resort of Bukovel.

It comes amid increasing concern over Russia ramping up hybrid threats including sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and potential drone incursions into NATO territory.

The meeting is also happening as overnight Russian strikes in multiple regions of Ukraine sparked fires, causing several deaths and injuries.

What is the 'Carpathian Eight'?

Dubbed the "Carpathian Eight,” the summit brought together nations such as Poland and Romania, who have been staunch supporters of Ukraine, along with others such as Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia, who have refused to provide Kyiv with direct military assistance.

Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the summit was a "significant beginning" of a movement intended to "further strengthen ties between our countries and create another strong element of cooperation at the EU level.”

The Ukrainian president added that the nations pledged to work together on security, energy, logistics, cross-border economic ties and support for local communities.

"The Carpathian macro-region has become one of the most reliable foundations of our defense. This is about strength that exists and will continue to exist," Zelenskyy added.

Ukraine secures nearly $4 billion in EU support

Zelenskyy said nearly 550 business representatives were expected to attend the forum and that investment ⁠and trade agreements worth €1

billion ($1.15 billion) would be signed.

"It's a ​good start: energy, logistics, infrastructure and cross-sector agreements," he said in a speech transmitted on Ukrainian TV.

As the summit kicked off, Zelenskyy announced in a Telegram post that Ukraine has secured €3.3 billion from an EU financial support package to strengthen Ukraine's defense capabilities.

The money included funds for the purchase of missiles and drones.

Poland joins anti-ballistic missile coalition

During the summit, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that his country had joined an anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine and other allies.

"From today, Poland is part of this major project ... we agreed on ‌the ⁠forms ⁠and frameworks of this cooperation," Tusk said in a video posted on X.

The air-defense coalition was created in July between Ukraine and nine other European countries. It would include the joint development of a new anti-ballistic missile system to serve ‌as ​an alternative and cheaper solution to the US Patriot system.

Tusk also announced that ​Poland has prepared a new "significant" aid package for Ukraine, without giving further detail.

"I will be very consistent ⁠here. ​No one will change my opinion ​that Poland has to support Ukraine in its war ​against Russian aggression ... History ‌cannot divide us vis-a-vis Russia today," Tusk said.

Zelenskyy thanked Poland for the new aid package.

"Ukraine and Poland ⁠are strong ​neighbors, friends, and partners, and we have one common enemy," he wrote on Telegram.

entries.title: German police probe arson attack on Wuppertal synagogue
entries.summary: The man detained shortly after allegedly trying to set fire to Wuppertal's synagogue made antisemitic comments to the arresting officers, prosecutors say. The 37-year-old Afghan citizen also had knives in his apartment.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

The man detained shortly after allegedly trying to set fire to Wuppertal's synagogue made antisemitic comments to the arresting officers, prosecutors say. The 37-year-old Afghan citizen also had knives in his apartment.

Prosecutors in the German city of Wuppertal said on Friday that they had taken over the lead in investigations into an attempted arson attack at the local synagogue.

They said a 37-year-old Afghan national arrested near the scene soon after made "comments that indicated an antisemitic motive" to detaining officers.

A search of his apartment uncovered weapons.

The suspect is being investigated for attempted aggravated arson. He was set to appear before a judge at an arraignment hearing on Friday.

What did prosecutors say about the incident and the investigation?

The attack took place midafternoon on Thursday. The suspect allegedly threw three containers of flammable liquid at a stairwell and doorway serving as an entrance to the synagogue and its adjoining eatery, Cafe Negev, and then set it alight.

The fire was quickly extinguished by a staff member, meaning that nobody was hurt and the damage to the structure was minimal, according to police.

"Shortly after, police officers on security duty on site were able to provisionally arrest a 37-year-old man in the immediate vicinity of the crime scene," Wuppertal's prosecutor's office said in a statement. "After reviewing the video surveillance footage from the scene he is strongly suspected of having laid the fire."

Although "intensive" background investigations were ongoing, prosecutors said there were already clues regarding the motive.

"During the police intervention, he issued comments that indicated an antisemitic motive for the crime," prosecutors wrote.

The Wuppertal resident with Afghan citizenship had a prior criminal record for threatening a female neighbor, they said.

"His apartment was already searched ... yesterday evening," prosecutors wrote. "Alongside documents several knives and a machete were located, which had been positioned in easy reach."

Police were investigating data from the suspect's mobile phone, which they confiscated in the arrest.

Central Council of Jews in Germany condemns nature of broad-daylight attack

Regional broadcaster WDR reported that about 30 people attended an impromptu gathering outside the synagogue on Thursday evening in a show of solidarity.

The Central Council of Jews in Germany condemned the attack in the buildup to the Yom Kippur religious holiday on September 20 and 21.

"Once again an attack on a synagogue has taken place at the time of Jewish high holidays," said Josef Schuster, the council's president.

"What disturbs me most is how coolly the perpetrator in Wuppertal carried out this attack in broad daylight. There's no sign of a sense of shame or being conscious of wrongdoing."

Wuppertal, home to around 350,000 people, lies just east of Düsseldorf in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
entries.summary: Buffett's son, Howard, will succeed him in the role. Buffett had earlier stepped down as Berkshire's CEO last year.
entries.content:
September 18, 2026

Buffett's son, Howard, will succeed him in the role. Buffett had earlier stepped down as Berkshire's CEO last year.

Billionaire investor and philanthropist Warren Buffett is stepping down as the chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, the holding company said Friday.

Buffett is 96 years old. His son, 71-year-old Howard Buffett, will succeed him in the role as chairman.

'I have never felt better about what comes next'

"I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett told shareholders in a message. "Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world. This is not something many people my age can say, and I have never felt better about what comes next."

This comes after Buffett stepped down as the firm's CEO last year, with Greg Abel succeeding him in that position. 

"Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values — both worth more than anything on our balance sheet," Buffett said. "Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against."

In a statement of his own, Abel said "the culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian."

How did Buffett lead Berkshire Hathaway?

Buffett purchased textile firm Berkshire Hathaway in 1965 and transformed it into a multinational conglomerate holding company with a worth of over $1 trillion (€871 billion) in terms of market capitalization. Most of the companies worth more than $1 trillion are in the tech sector.

Buffett's investment prowess has led to Berkshire beating the S&P market index in 40 out of the past 60 years.

Berkshire owns whole businesses in sectors such as insurance and energy; the firm also owns restaurant chain Dairy Queen. Moreover, Berkshire invests in companies such as Apple, Coca-Cola, Chevron and Bank of America.  

According to Forbes, Buffett is the 10th-richest person in the world today with a net worth of $144.7 billion.

Buffett grew up in Omaha, Nebraska, where Berkshire is also headquartered. Known as the "Oracle of Omaha," Buffett has embraced a folksy public persona and is enamored with American staples such as McDonald's breakfasts, Dairy Queen sundaes and Coca Cola.

Edited by: Zac Crellin
